rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Classical commentators read Moses’ words physically: the Israelites were coming behind him and were close by.
rows.anchor: The classical commentators understand this phrase in its physical sense

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the phrase figuratively: Moses assumed Israel would follow his guidance in his absence; Moses was alone on the ascent, and the sequel disproves his assumption.
rows.anchor: Moses was obviously meant to be alone on his ascent of Mount Sinai

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says as-samiri is an adjectival noun indicating the person’s descent or origin.
rows.anchor: The designation as-samiri is undoubtedly an adjectival noun denoting the person's descent or origin

rows.speaker: Tabari and Zamakhshari
rows.claim: They explain the designation as a man from the Jewish clan of Samirah, later known as the Samaritans, though that sect did not yet exist in Moses’ time.
rows.anchor: According to one of the explanations advanced by Tabari and Zamakhshari, it signifies

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas (Razi)
rows.claim: Ibn 'Abbas suggests the man was an Egyptian convert who joined Israel’s exodus; Asad connects samiri possibly with Egyptian shemer, “foreigner” or “stranger.”
rows.anchor: as Ibn 'Abbas maintained (Razi) - the person in question was one of the many Egyptians

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the golden calf episode echoes Egypt’s Apis cult, strengthening the Egyptian-origin possibility.
rows.anchor: This surmise is strengthened by his introduction of the worship of the golden calf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad allows that later Samaritans may have descended, or been reputed to descend, from this man; this could partly explain their lasting antagonism with the wider Israelite community.
rows.anchor: it is not impossible that the latter-day Samaritans descended - or were reputed to descend

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari offers “Did the time of my absence seem too long to you?”; Asad notes that ahd can mean a period as well as a covenant or promise.
rows.anchor: according to Zamakhshari: "Did, then, the time [of my absence] seem too long to you?"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the question as asking whether the people are determined to disregard the consequences of their actions.
rows.anchor: are you determined to disregard the consequences of your doings?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic eschatology depicts the world’s end as a fundamental, cataclysmic transformation of the physical universe, not its annihilation; 14:48 describes earth and heavens becoming another earth and heavens.
rows.anchor: the "end of the world" does not signify an annihilation - i.e., reduction to nothingness - of the physical universe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad identifies the caller who permits no deviation as the summons to the Last Judgment.
rows.anchor: i.e., the summons to the Last Judgment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the Qur’anic concept of intercession at Judgment, Asad directs readers to his note on 10:3.
rows.anchor: Regarding the Qur'anic concept of "intercession" on the Day of Judgment, see note 7 on 10:3.

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas (as quoted by Baghawi)
rows.claim: Ibn 'Abbas takes the accepted “word” as a metonym for belief that no deity exists save God, realizing His oneness and uniqueness.
rows.anchor: according to Ibn 'Abbas (as quoted by Baghawi) - a metonym for the belief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad takes the verse’s scope as all mankind and links this universal principle to 7:158.
rows.anchor: I.e., towards all mankind. For an elucidation of this fundamental principle underlying the message of the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an addresses people regardless of descent, race, or cultural environment.
rows.anchor: its appeal to all mankind irrespective of descent, race or cultural environment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its appeal rests exclusively on human reason and therefore asks no one to accept dogma through blind faith.
rows.anchor: it appeals exclusively to man's reason and, hence, does not postulate any dogma that could be accepted on the basis of blind faith alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the Qur’an’s wording has remained unchanged since revelation and will remain protected, citing 15:9; these factors make it the final revelation, and Muhammad the last prophet, the “seal” (33:40).
rows.anchor: the fact that - contrary to all other sacred scriptures known to history - the Qur'an has remained entirely unchanged in its wording

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says ‘ala sawa combines fairness through a clear, unambiguous announcement with equality, since it is addressed alike to all human beings.
rows.anchor: comprises in this context two distinct concepts: that of fairness as regards the clarity and unambiguity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders ‘ala as “against” what people attribute to God by way of description or definition; only divine grace can save humans from anthropomorphic definitions of the transcendent, infinite, unfathomable God, prompted by human weakness.
rows.anchor: only God's grace can save man from the blasphemous attempts - prompted by his inherent weakness - to bring God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sacrifice is a conscious, selfless offering in God’s name of something valued, not an effort to propitiate a deity imagined to have human emotions; see also 22:36.
rows.anchor: as a conscious, selfless offering in His name of something that one cherishes as necessary and valuable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad clarifies that the phrase is literally “of them.”
rows.anchor: Lit., "of them".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the connective as “thus.”
rows.anchor: Lit., "thus".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to the sacrificial animals.
rows.anchor: I.e., the sacrificial animals.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses and Aaron are named because, unlike other prophets, they were rejected by their community’s oppressors rather than by their own community.
rows.anchor: Moses and Aaron are mentioned here by name because their case was different from that of all other prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad notes that mubin can mean both “manifest” and “manifesting,” while al-haqq is rendered “the Ultimate Truth,” with links to his notes on 12:1 and 20:114.
rows.anchor: Regarding the double meaning ("manifest" and "manifesting") inherent in the adjective mubin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here the active sense “manifesting” refers to God revealing on Judgment Day the true nature of people’s deeds and the enormity of the sin under discussion.
rows.anchor: the active form of mubin ("manifesting") apparently relates to God's revelation, on Judgment Day, of the true nature of man's actions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses “even less conscious of the right way” as being farther astray from the path of truth, linking 7:179.
rows.anchor: Lit., "they are farther astray from the path [of truth]": see note 144 on 7:179.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad explains that the ignorant address the servants of the Most Gracious to ridicule them or argue against their beliefs.
rows.anchor: with the aim to ridicule them or to argue against their beliefs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links Moses’ sudden realization that killing the Egyptian was a grievous sin to 28:15–16 and his note on 28:15.
rows.anchor: after having killed the Egyptian, Moses suddenly realized that he had committed a grievous sin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s question refers to the terms in which Moses was instructed to announce his mission and apparently did so, as stated in 26:16.
rows.anchor: A reference to the terms in which Moses was to - and apparently did - announce his mission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says Moses’ appeal to God’s creative will evidenced in all existence is a main reason this surah retells his story, also pointing to 26:28.
rows.anchor: by the evidence of His creative will in all that exists

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal “Do you not hear?” is rhetorical, conveying astonishment, indignation, or derision; Asad idiomatically translates it “Did you hear what he said?”
rows.anchor: a rhetorical question meant to convey astonishment, indignation or derision
